titleStmt.title: Memorandum From the President’s Assistant for National Security Affairs (Carlucci) to President Reagan

div.head: 390. Memorandum From the President’s Assistant for National Security Affairs (Carlucci) to President Reagan
div.p: Ecuadoran President Leon Febres-Cordero has been taken hostage by elements of Ecuador’s Air Force. You may recall the successful State Visit last January we had with this pro-U.S., pro-free market Latin American President.

Along with the President, the Chairman of the Ecuadoran Joint Chiefs of Staff and the three chiefs of their armed services were taken hostage. These events occurred this morning at Taura Air Force Base near Guayaquil, Ecuador. The renegade Air Force elements are supporters of Air Force General Vargas, who staged a mutiny in March 1986 and is currently in prison. This issue has become a contentious legislative/executive confrontation in Ecuador because the leftist-opposition controlled Congress has voted that Vargas be amnestied, but Febres-Cordero has refused to implement this citing the act unconstitutional.

The State Department has issued a strong statement in support of Ecuador’s constitutional democracy and urged the unconditional release of Ecuador’s democratically elected President. We have requested the White House Press Office to make a similar statement.

In response to a request from the Government of Ecuador, US Ambassador to Ecuador, Fred Rondon, has authorized a US Air Force pilot to fly an Ecuadoran C–130 transport aircraft to ferry Ecuadoran Army Special Forces personnel to a secure area in Guayaquil. Ambassador Rondon has stressed that this action will not take the US pilot to any scene of potential conflict. The Government of Ecuador has also requested a few US hostage rescue experts to advise them on how to proceed. We are currently studying this request.

note.p: Source: Reagan Library, NSC Records, Latin American Affairs Directorate, Country File, Ecuador (1/16/1987). Secret. A stamped notation at the top of the memorandum reads: “The President has seen 1/20.” Reagan wrote his initials at the top of the page. Tillman sent the memorandum to Carlucci for signature under cover of an undated memorandum, along with telegram 590 from Quito, January 16, in which Rondon described the transport arranged for the Ecuadorian Special Forces. Rondon commented: “This will convey strongest possible message to Ecuadorean army that we support army effort to rescue President and uphold constitutional order.”

See footnotes 2 and 3, Document 389. A January 16 White House Situation Room Note stated that “Vargas reportedly has left his barracks and been taken by helicopter to an undisclosed location” and that Febres-Cordero had “issued a statement from Taura airbase which asked the Ecuadorean people to remain calm” and “gave instructions to the military to stop their mobilization.” (Ibid)

In telegram 15855 to all American Republic posts, January 16, the Department wrote: “At 0830 on January 16 President Leon Febres Cordero of Ecuador was taken hostage by a rebellious air force unit near Guayaquil. The USG is calling for his immediate and unconditional release. If appropriate and if you have not already done so, you are requested to contact host governments to urge immediate statements calling for the release of President Febres Cordero.” The Department also included the text of its statement, including: “We call upon those holding the President and his aides to release them immediately and abide by the constitution and the democratic process in Ecuador.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D870042–0656)

Request has not been found. Febres-Cordero was freed after he ordered Vargas’ release and pledged not to punish his captors. (See Jorge Ribadeneira, “Ecuadorean President Seized, Freed,” Washington Post, January 17, 1987, p. A13) In telegram 102 from Guayaquil, January 17, the Consulate wrote that Febres-Cordero had stated “that he is convinced that Vargas’ instructions to the mutineers was assassinate the president—not to capture him. The paratroopers opened fire indiscriminately at the group and did not kill the president only because when he was not hit in the first volley they would have had to have shot him lying on the ground in full view of a ‘comitiva’ of more than 25 dignitaries and media reps. LFC believes the exchange of prisoners was improvised when the rebels found themselves with a live Febres-Cordero on their hands. He added that when it occurred, there were people in Quito who acted as if his government was at an end and were discussing formation of a new administration.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, N870001–0285)

In telegram 673 from Quito, January 18, Rondon reported that he had met on January 17 with Ecuadorian Government Minister Lucho Robles who said “that Febres Cordero was shattered by his experience in Taura” and “dumbfounded by the fact that it took 12 hours to free him.” Robles also commented that the “President appears to have thought his government would not act to liberate him.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D870042–0656) Reagan called Febres-Cordero on January 20, from 12:02 until 12:05 p.m., to share his relief that Febres-Cordero “emerged unharmed.” (Memorandum of Conversation, January 20; Reagan Library, NSC Records, Latin American Affairs Directorate, Action File, Ecuador (01/16/1987–04/02/1987))
